newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-France names two to central bank council.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-France names two to central bank council.

text.p: The French government on Friday named two new members to the Bank of France's key policy council in a move which could shift the balance of power at the independent central bank in favour of lower interest rates.

Government spokesman Alain Lamassoure said Pierre Guillen, 69, ex-deputy head of the employers' federation CNPF, and Jean-Rene Bernard, 64, former deputy governor at property lender Credit Foncier, had been appointed to the nine-member monetary policy council.
He said there would be no change in policy and told reporters President Jacques Chirac had expressed confidence in the independent Bank of France to continue a stable and steady monetary policy.
But economists said the appointments could shift the bias in favour of slightly faster interest rate cuts.
Both men are seen as Chirac's personal choice, thereby increasing the government's leverage over the Bank of France, until now dominated by its hawkish governor Jean-Claude Trichet.
Financial markets have been watching the decision closely for any sign of a softening in the Bank's commitment to defending the stability of the franc against the mark.
The new members, viewed by economists as potentially more dovish on monetary policy, replace ex-journalist Jean Boissonnat and ex-banker Bruno de Maulde, whose mandates expire next week.
The two were seen as strong backers of the existing policy of maintaining French interest rates slightly above those in Germany to protect the franc's stability against the mark.
Asked by reporters whether the appointments indicated a shift in policy, Prime Minister Alain Juppe replied, "No, no, not at all. Rather the contrary."

Guillen, 69, said last month he was "radically against" devaluing the franc but, that "like many industrialists, I wanted interest rates to come down a little bit faster, but that's an opinion...of a representative of industry."

Bernard, 64, whose son-in-law is deputy secretary-general in President Jacques Chirac's office, is not thought to have any strong convictions on monetary policy. But he is close to Chirac and would be expected to follow the president's lead on policy, sources close to the selection process say.

The French franc weakened on the news, easing to 3.3772 per mark, down more than half a centime against its level late on Thursday. Bonds showed little reaction to the appointments but stocks rose slightly on the hope of lower interest rates.

The appointment of the two new members is likely to create a new balance of power in the council, which until now had a six to three majority in favour of the existing cautious policy on interest rates, sources close to the Bank say.
Guillen is seen likely to join ranks with members who have called publicly for faster rate cuts to boost growth and bring down unemployment, running at a record 12.7 percent.
One of these, Paul Marchelli, told Reuters on Friday he still saw room to cut rates, but this must be done carefully.
He said, however, there was no chance of seeing a majority emerge at the Bank of France in favour of weakening the franc. "It is completely unthinkable," he said.
According to one banker, the key question is whether France tries to reduce official rates below those of Germany.

"The nominations which have just been made at the Bank of France clearly signify one thing, that a decision has been made to bring French short-term rates below German rates in the coming months," Jean-Michel Naulot, a banker close to National Assembly President Philippe Seguin who has called for stronger action on employment, told Reuters.
Bernard, whose views on monetary policy are less well known, is likely to be the swing member in an otherwise four-to-four balance between doves and hawks on the council.
Economists said they did not believe there was necessarily any radical change of policy in the offing right away.

"I don't think it will change the broad lines of exchange rate policy. The French franc will remain pegged to the deutsche mark within the former bands of the ERM (exchange rate mechanism)," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said.
Chirac has repeatedly stated his commitment to a stable currency and is seen as unlikely to want to endanger the franc-mark link, the cornerstone of the future European single currency.
